Transdermal uptake of drugs is generally achieved through the application of patches. 

Transdermal uptake is governed by Fick’s law of diffusion and physiological factors.

Fick’s Law of diffusion states that:

D = ΔP.k.A/ t

ΔP = Drug concentration gradient over the skin/membrane, increasing drug concentration →↑ rate of diffusion

A = membrane diffusion area, size of patch/skin area covered

k= diffusion constant = solubility/square rootMW, increasing lipid solubility of the drug would increase the rate of diffusion through the skin   

t= Membrane thickness, thicker skin results in slower diffusion of drug 

Physiologically uptake from the skin is also dependant of skin blood flow to maintain the concentration gradient across the skin, ↓blood flow would result in closer equalisation of drug concentration over the skin and ↓diffusion

Advantages:

Maintains steady plasma concentration of drug due constant dosing/administration, even with agents with shorter half-lives. 

Avoids side effects of peak concentrations

Patient compliance easier - no forgotten dose or different timing

Avoids first ass metabolism 

Disadvantages:

Drug must be lipid soluble - not suitable to all medications 

Slow Onset and Offset - takes much longer to reach effective concentrations, usually not useful in acute setting. 

Patch may be forgotten to be swapped removed 

Temperature may alter absorption rate
